input:
Basis

This report sets out the design of an amine absorber intended for gas treatment service, and it is hoped that the following sections will provide a comprehensive overview of the basis, the sizing, the materials selection, and the principal risks that have been identified to date. The absorber works by bringing the incoming gas into contact with a circulating amine solvent, which absorbs the key component from the gas stream. The design throughput is 58 t of gas per day, and the removal duty is 93% of the key component in the feed gas, figures which together define the overall duty that the unit is required to perform. The rich solvent leaves from the base of the absorber and passes onwards to regeneration, while the treated gas leaves from the top of the column. It should be noted that this report is concerned with the absorber itself; the regeneration equipment, although closely related, is dealt with elsewhere in the design package. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel, and this grade is stated here, in the basis, so that the materials section can build upon it. The basis of design takes the feed gas at its stated throughput and composition as received, with no pretreatment within the absorber battery limits other than the inlet separation that is needed in order to protect the packing from liquid carryover. The operating pressure and temperature are those of the upstream unit which delivers the gas, and the absorber has been designed for the full range of conditions that that unit can present, including upset conditions, rather than for one nominal operating point alone. The design follows the applicable pressure equipment code for the vessel, together with the project specifications covering internals, nozzles, and instrumentation. Pressure relief is provided in accordance with the relief design for the unit, and the absorber is protected against overpressure arising from blocked outlets and from the connected regeneration system. Instrumentation includes level control on the sump, differential pressure measurement across the packed bed, temperature measurements at the gas inlet and outlet and in the liquid distributors, and sampling points on both the lean and the rich solvent lines, all of which will play an important role in the safe and effective operation of the unit.

Sizing

The absorber takes the form of a packed column, which was selected after careful consideration of the alternatives. The diameter is set by the vapour load at the base of the bed, where the gas flow is at its highest, and it has been chosen in such a way that the operating point sits comfortably clear of flooding at the design throughput, with the margin required by the project specification. Particular attention has been paid to the rich end of the column, because the rich solvent has the higher viscosity and also the greater tendency to foam, and it is by no means automatic that a diameter which proves adequate at the top of the bed will also prove adequate at the bottom. The packing is a structured packing, selected on account of its low pressure drop and its good liquid-spreading characteristics at the liquid rates in question. The design of the distributor forms an integral part of the sizing, since maldistribution can waste bed depth more rapidly than any other single defect. The bed depth is set by the transfer requirement associated with the stated removal duty, and has been worked out from the equilibrium behaviour of the solvent system together with the approach to equilibrium that the design is prepared to claim; a conservative approach has deliberately been adopted, so that the resulting depth reflects the uncertainty present in the underlying rate data. The pressure drop across the bed at the design point is low by design, and the margin between the operating pressure drop and the flooding pressure drop is reported alongside the hydraulic calculation. The sump has been sized so as to hold the inventory needed for the level control to ride through the disturbances produced by the upstream unit, and the nozzles have been sized in line with the velocity limits set out in the project specification for gas and liquid lines. The question of turndown is addressed in the risks section; the sizing itself is stated at the design throughput, with the distributor turndown range being stated by the vendor as part of the internals package.

Materials

As stated in the basis, the wetted parts are the stainless steel grade specified there, and this section explains the reasoning behind that choice. Amine service presents a number of corrosion challenges which need to be properly understood. The amine itself can be handled readily enough, but the degradation products and heat-stable salts which gradually accumulate in a working solvent are known to attack carbon steel and, at higher temperatures and concentrations, can attack stainless grades as well. The choice of a stainless grade for the wetted parts is therefore fundamentally a corrosion decision rather than a pressure decision. Within the wider circuit, the reboiler and the hot rich-solvent lines are the locations giving greatest cause for concern, while within the absorber itself it is the distributor and the packing support which see the richest and warmest liquid. The packing itself is supplied in the same grade family as the shell, so that the internals and the vessel will age together and no galvanic couple is set up between them. Gasket materials at the flanged joints have been selected on the basis of temperature limit and resistance to the amine, and the bolting has been specified for the flange class and the service temperature in question. External surfaces are coated in order to provide protection against the atmosphere. Corrosion monitoring is carried out by means of solvent analysis during operation: the solvent is sampled on a regular cycle and its degradation state, iron content, and heat-stable salt level are all tracked, since a rising trend in any of these provides the earliest indication that the circuit is corroding somewhere, long before a wall thickness measurement would show it. Finally, inspection access is provided at the sump and at the distributor level, so that the internals can be examined at turnaround without any need to cut the vessel.

Risks

There are two items which remain open at the close of this report, namely fouling and turndown, and it is important to be clear that neither of them is resolved here. Fouling is an open item because the feed gas, as received, carries with it whatever the upstream unit sends, and the rate at which deposits form on the packing and in the distributor in this particular service has not been established by the operating data currently available. Deposits have the effect of raising the pressure drop across the bed and disturbing the liquid distribution, so fouling tends to show itself first as a hydraulic symptom and only later as a loss of removal duty; by the time the duty actually falls, the bed is already badly distributed. The design incorporates those mitigations which do not depend on knowing the rate in question: a differential pressure measurement across the bed with an alarm on the trend, access for washing, and an inlet separator to keep liquid carryover out of the packing. What is missing at this stage is a defensible cleaning interval, and that can only really come from operating experience on this gas, or from a pilot run carried out on a slipstream of it. Turndown is an open item because the absorber has been sized at the design throughput, and the behaviour of the packed bed at low rates is governed by the liquid distributor, whose effective range is a vendor figure rather than a measured one for this particular combination of packing and solvent. At low liquid rates there is a risk that the packing will run partly dry, in which case the removal duty falls away faster than the throughput does. The operating range which the unit can honestly claim has therefore not yet been established, and the low-rate behaviour will need either vendor test data on the selected distributor, or acceptance testing during commissioning, before the range is published to operations. Both items will remain on the risk register until such time as the evidence described above actually exists.

This report covers the design of an amine absorber for gas treatment service. The design throughput is 58 t of gas per day, and the removal duty is 93% of the key component in the feed gas. The rich solvent leaving the absorber base passes to regeneration, and the treated gas leaves at the absorber top; the absorber itself is sized and specified here, and the regeneration equipment is covered elsewhere in the design package. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; the grade is stated here once and is the grade the materials section works from. The basis of design is the feed gas at its stated throughput and composition as received, without pretreatment inside the absorber battery limits beyond the inlet separation needed to protect the packing from liquid carryover. Operating pressure and temperature are those of the upstream unit that delivers the gas, and the absorber is designed for the full range of conditions that unit can present, including its upset conditions, rather than for a single nominal point. The design follows the applicable pressure equipment code for the vessel and the project specifications for internals, nozzles, and instrumentation. The design life of the vessel and its internals is the project design life, and the corrosion allowance, the fatigue assessment where the code requires one, and the inspection provisions in this report are all set against that life rather than against the first turnaround.

Sizing

The absorber is a packed column. Diameter is set by the vapour load at the base of the bed, where the gas flow is highest, and is chosen so that the operating point sits clear of flooding at the design throughput with the margin the project specification requires. The flooding margin is held at the rich end of the column because the rich solvent has the higher viscosity and the greater foaming tendency, and a diameter that is adequate at the top of the bed is not automatically adequate at the bottom. Packing is a structured packing selected for low pressure drop and good liquid spreading at the liquid rates in question; the distributor design is part of the sizing, since maldistribution wastes bed depth faster than any other single defect. Bed depth is set by the transfer requirement for the stated removal duty, worked out from the equilibrium behaviour of the solvent system and the approach to equilibrium the design is prepared to claim; the claimed approach is a conservative one, and the resulting depth carries the uncertainty in the underlying rate data. Turndown is addressed in the risks section; the sizing itself is stated at the design throughput, with the distributor turndown range stated by the vendor as part of the internals package. Liquid holdup in the bed is a secondary sizing output: it sets the solvent inventory in the column, the response time of the sump level to a change in circulation rate, and the quantity of solvent that drains to the sump on a trip, and the sump sizing takes the drained inventory as its governing case.
